title: A Scorebook and a Diamond Plan
bigQuestion: How did writing games down and drawing fields on paper let faraway towns share one game?

story.title: A Pencil on the Page
story.kicker: On a bench beside a chalked field, a scorebook waits for the first inning.
paragraphs: It is a spring afternoon at a high school field in central Illinois. A fresh chalk line runs from home plate out to left field. On the bench sits a thick scorebook, open to a clean page. A yellow pencil lies across it.

Mr. Okafor, a history teacher, keeps score for the school team. He writes the date at the top. He fills in the two school names and the list of batters. Each batter gets a row. Each inning gets a column of small boxes.
A fifth grader named Jada is visiting with her older brother. She leans over the page. "Why write it all down?" she asks. "Everyone can see who wins."

Mr. Okafor turns back a few pages. There are last week's game, and the one before that. "People who were not here can read this," he says. "The other school will send its numbers too. Then the whole conference can compare."

He points to a folded paper tucked in the back cover. It is a drawing of the field, seen from above, with every distance written in feet. "The book tells what happened," he says. "The plan tells where it happened."
story.think: Why might a written record of a game matter to people who were never at the field?

lessons.title: The Club's Own Books
lessons.mainIdea: The Knickerbocker club wrote down its games by hand in books starting in the 1840s.
reading: The Knickerbocker Base Ball Club did more than write rules. From the 1840s, members also kept handwritten game books. After each game, someone wrote the date and the players' names. They noted how many runs each player scored and how many times he was out.

These books are some of the oldest baseball records in the United States. Some of their pages survive today in library collections in New York. Historians use them to learn who played, when and how often.

A game book turned a single afternoon into a lasting record. A club could look back at a whole season. It could see which members came most often. The books show that members often played games among themselves, not only against other clubs.

words.d: a book in which a club wrote down each game's date, players and runs
a written account that keeps facts after an event is over
the part of the year when a club or league plays its games

look.prompt: What can a historian learn from this page? What can the page not tell us?

check.why: The club's game books listed the date, the players and their runs and outs.

check.q: Where do some of the Knickerbocker game book pages survive today?

check.why: Surviving pages are kept in library collections in New York.

check.q: What is a record?
choices: a written account that keeps facts after an event
check.why: A record keeps the facts after the game is over.

lessons.title: Henry Chadwick's Box Score
lessons.mainIdea: Henry Chadwick, a New York writer, helped create the box score so newspaper readers could follow games.
reading: Henry Chadwick was born in England in 1824. His family moved to Brooklyn, New York, when he was a boy. He grew up knowing cricket, an English game that already kept careful written scores. In the 1850s, he began writing about baseball for New York newspapers, including the New York Clipper.

Chadwick helped shape the *box score*. A box score is a small table printed in a newspaper. It lists each player with numbers such as runs, hits and outs. A reader in another town can see what happened without being at the field.

Chadwick also wrote early baseball guides and argued for clear rules. He is often credited with using the letter K to mark a strikeout in a scorebook. He died in 1908. In 1938, he was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame. In his lifetime, many people called him the Father of Baseball.

words.d: a small printed table listing each player's numbers from one game
an English-born New York writer (1824–1908) who helped create the box score

look.title: Reading a small table

look.prompt: If you missed the game, what could you find out from this table?

choices: a table of each player's numbers from one game
check.why: A box score is a printed table of players and numbers from a game.

check.q: Which game did Chadwick know first, which already kept written scores?
check.why: Chadwick grew up with cricket, which already kept careful scores.

check.q: Why was the box score useful?
choices: it let readers far away follow a game
check.why: Readers who were not at the field could see what happened.

lessons.title: Innings in a Grid
lessons.mainIdea: A scorebook page uses rows for batters and columns for innings so a whole game fits on one sheet.
reading: After 1857, a game had nine innings and each side had nine players. Scorebooks were printed to match. A page has a *grid*, which is a set of rows and columns. Each batter gets a row. Each inning gets a column.

Scorekeepers use short marks to fit a lot on one page. Many give each fielding position a number from 1 to 9. The pitcher is 1 and the catcher is 2. These numbers let a scorer write down who made each out in a tiny box.

A finished page shows the whole game at once. Totals at the bottom add up the runs in each inning. At the end, a scorer can copy the totals into a box score. Printed scorecards were also sold at ballparks, so fans could keep their own records.

words.d: a set of rows and columns that makes small boxes on a page
the person who writes down what happens in a game
a printed card or page for keeping score of one game, often sold at ballparks

look.title: Rows and columns
look.text: A scorebook page has nine rows, one for each batter. It has nine columns, one for each inning. The row for the third batter and the column for the fourth inning meet in one small box.
look.prompt: What does that one box tell you? Why is a grid a good shape for a nine-inning game?

check.q: In a scorebook grid, what does each column usually stand for?
check.why: Each inning gets a column; each batter gets a row.

check.q: In the common scorer's numbers, which position is 1?
check.why: Scorers often number the pitcher 1 and the catcher 2.

check.q: Why were scorebooks printed with nine columns?
choices: because 1857 rules made games nine innings
because there were nine clubs in 1845
because bases were nine feet apart
because the IHSA began with nine schools
check.why: The 1857 rules set nine innings, so pages had nine columns.

lessons.title: Rules in Print
lessons.mainIdea: Cheap printed guides carried baseball rules and records to towns far from New York.
reading: In 1860, a New York publisher named Beadle began selling *Beadle's Dime Base-Ball Player*. It cost ten cents. Henry Chadwick edited it. It printed the rules of the clubs' national association, along with club news and records of past games.

A small guide could travel by train and mail. A club in a new town could read the same rules as a club in Brooklyn. During the Civil War, from 1861 to 1865, soldiers helped carry the game to army camps and back to their home towns.

In the late 1870s, Albert Spalding began printing *Spalding's Official Base Ball Guide* in Chicago. It came out every year for decades. It printed the National League rules and a year of records. Guides like these helped one written game spread across the country.

words.d: a printed booklet with rules, records and news about a sport
a ten-cent guide first sold in 1860 and edited by Henry Chadwick
a yearly guide printed in Chicago by Albert Spalding's company, starting in the late 1870s

check.q: Who edited Beadle's Dime Base-Ball Player?
check.why: Henry Chadwick edited the Beadle guide, first sold in 1860.

check.q: Where was Spalding's Official Base Ball Guide printed?
check.why: Spalding's company printed the guide in Chicago.

check.q: How did printed guides help baseball spread?
choices: clubs far away could read the same rules and records

check.why: Guides carried the same rules and records by train and mail.

lessons.title: Standings and a Pennant
lessons.mainIdea: The National League, begun in 1876, kept a table of wins and losses to decide its champion.
reading: On February 2, 1876, club owners met at a hotel in New York City. They formed the *National League*. William Hulbert, who ran the Chicago club, led the effort. Eight clubs joined in the first season.

A league needs a fair way to choose a champion. The National League kept *standings*. Standings are a table that lists every club's wins and losses. The club with the best record at the end of the season won the pennant, a long flag that stood for the title.

Chicago's club, then called the White Stockings, won the first pennant in 1876. It finished with 52 wins and 14 losses. Albert Spalding was its star pitcher and manager. That club is the ancestor of today's Chicago Cubs.

words.d: a baseball league formed on February 2, 1876; it is still one of the two major leagues
a table that lists every team's wins and losses
a long flag given to a league champion; also the title itself

look.prompt: Why does a league need a written table like this instead of just one final game?

check.q: Who led the founding of the National League?
check.why: William Hulbert of the Chicago club led the effort in 1876.

check.q: What are standings?
choices: a table of each team's wins and losses
check.why: Standings list every team's wins and losses.

check.q: Which club won the first National League pennant in 1876?
check.why: Chicago's club finished 52 and 14 and won the 1876 pennant.

lessons.title: Records Older Than the Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Written records let Illinois schools compare results, and some records are older than the association itself.
reading: In 1900, Illinois high schools formed the Illinois High School Association, or *IHSA*. It sets rules for school sports and runs state championships. Before 1900, some schools already met to compete in track and field.

The IHSA keeps lists of past champions. Its track and field records name state champions from 1893, seven years before the association existed. Someone wrote those early results down. The IHSA later added them to its own lists.

Other sports came later. The IHSA's first boys tennis champion was crowned in 1912. Illinois held its first state baseball tournament in 1940, and Belleville won it. The IHSA took charge of that tournament in 1941. Each year's results go into the same records, so a school today can compare itself with schools from long ago.

words.d: the Illinois High School Association, formed in 1900, which runs Illinois high school state championships
the winner of a contest, such as a state tournament

check.q: Which school won the first Illinois state baseball tournament, in 1940?
check.why: Belleville won the first state baseball tournament in 1940. The IHSA took charge of the tournament in 1941.

lessons.title: The Rule Book Diagram
lessons.mainIdea: The Official Baseball Rules include a drawing of the field with its measured distances.
reading: The Official Baseball Rules begin with the field itself. A rule called "Layout of the Field" lists the distances. It comes with a *diagram*, a drawing of the field seen from above. Builders can use it to lay out a new diamond.

The diagram shows bases 90 feet apart. The distance straight from home plate to second base is about 127 feet 3 inches. The pitcher's plate sits 60 feet 6 inches from home. Lines called *foul lines* run from home past first and third base.

The rules also set sizes for new major league parks. Parks built after June 1, 1958, must reach at least 325 feet down each foul line. They must reach at least 400 feet to center field. Older parks, like Chicago's Wrigley Field, were built long before this rule.

words.d: a drawing that shows how something is laid out, often from above
the two lines from home plate past first and third base that mark the edges of fair ground

choices: it was built long before the 1958 rule

check.why: The rule covers parks built after June 1, 1958; Wrigley Field opened in 1914.

lessons.title: Chicago Builds Ballparks
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's major league clubs moved from wooden grounds to large parks built in 1910 and 1914.
reading: In October 1871, the Great Chicago Fire burned much of the city. It destroyed the White Stockings' ballpark and their equipment. The club did not play in 1872 or 1873. It came back in 1874 on new grounds.
Early ballparks were mostly wood, and many burned. In the 1900s, owners began building parks of steel and concrete. The Chicago White Sox opened *Comiskey Park* on the South Side on July 1, 1910.

On the North Side, a park opened in 1914 for a club called the Chicago Whales. It was called Weeghman Park. The Cubs moved there in 1916. In 1926, it was renamed Wrigley Field, after the club's owner, William Wrigley Jr.

words.d: the October 1871 fire that burned much of Chicago, including its ballpark
the White Sox ballpark on Chicago's South Side, opened in 1910
the Cubs' ballpark on Chicago's North Side, opened in 1914 as Weeghman Park

lessons.title: A Scoreboard for Everyone
lessons.mainIdea: A big scoreboard turns the scorebook into a public record the whole crowd can read.
reading: A scorebook is small. Only the person holding it can read it during the game. A *scoreboard* is a large sign that shows the score to everyone in the park. It lists runs by inning, just like the bottom of a scorebook page.

In 1937, the Cubs built a large scoreboard above the center field bleachers at Wrigley Field. It is still worked by hand. Workers inside slide metal number plates into place as the game goes on. It also shows scores from games in other cities.

The same year, the club planted ivy on the outfield brick walls. Bill Veeck, a young club worker, helped with the project. Both the ivy and the hand-turned scoreboard became well-known parts of the park.

words.d: a large sign at a field that shows the score to the whole crowd
rows of simple, uncovered seats, often in the outfield

check.why: A scoreboard shows the score to everyone in the park.

lessons.title: A Line in the Records
lessons.mainIdea: Black players were shut out of the major league records for decades, so they built leagues and records of their own.
reading: In December 1867, the National Association of Base Ball Players refused to admit the Pythian Base Ball Club of Philadelphia. The Pythians were a Black club. The association's committee said it would not accept clubs with Black players. This unfair barrier is called the *color line*.

Moses Fleetwood Walker played in the major leagues for Toledo in 1884. By the late 1880s, owners had pushed Black players out. Cap Anson, the star of Chicago's club, refused to play against Black players in those years.

In 1920, Rube Foster, owner of the Chicago American Giants, helped found the *Negro National League*. Black newspapers such as the Chicago Defender printed its scores. In 2020, Major League Baseball named the Negro Leagues of 1920 to 1948 as major leagues. In 2024, their players' numbers joined the official major league records.

words.d: an unfair barrier that kept Black players out of white clubs and leagues
a league of Black clubs founded in 1920 with Rube Foster of Chicago as a leader
owner of the Chicago American Giants who helped found the Negro National League in 1920

check.q: Who helped found the Negro National League in 1920?
check.why: Rube Foster of the Chicago American Giants helped found it in 1920.

check.q: What happened to Negro League records in 2024?

check.why: In 2024, Negro League players' numbers joined the official major league records.

lessons.title: Women on the Scorecard
lessons.mainIdea: Women played baseball from the 1860s, and a women's professional league played in Illinois from 1943 to 1954.
reading: In 1866, students at Vassar College, a women's college in New York, formed baseball clubs. Some people at the time said sports were not proper for women. The students played anyway, on the college grounds.

In 1943, many men were away fighting in World War II. Philip K. Wrigley, owner of the Chicago Cubs, started the *All-American Girls Professional Baseball League*. It played until 1954. Its teams were in Midwest cities.

The Rockford Peaches of Rockford, Illinois, played in the league for all of its seasons. They won several league championships. The league kept its own records and box scores. Most of its players were white; Black women were not signed by the league.

words.d: a women's professional league started by Philip K. Wrigley that played from 1943 to 1954
a team from Rockford, Illinois, in the women's professional league
